claim: Subdivision Surface (Catmull-Clark) recursively splits each polygon into smaller quads while averaging vertex positions toward their neighbors, turning sharp angular edges into smooth curves non-destructively. Keeping the base mesh itself low-poly while relying on the modifier to generate a smooth, high-density result at render time keeps editing, UV unwrapping, and deformation/rigging fast and simple, since all of those operate on the low-poly cage, not the evaluated high-density result.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 24:20-25:52, the Subdivision Surface modifier's viewport levels are stepped from 0 (raw low-poly torus) up to 1, 2, 3, with a zoomed-in single quad shown splitting into 4 smaller quads and a diagram of a sharp 90-degree corner's vertices being pulled inward and averaged toward neighbors.
rejected_alternative: Modeling directly at high polygon density instead of a low-poly cage plus a Subdivision Surface modifier
reason: A high-density base mesh makes every downstream operation (editing, UV unwrapping, rigging/deformation) slower and more error-prone than working on a simple low-poly cage and letting the modifier generate the smooth result only when actually needed (viewport/render).

claim: Modifiers execute strictly top-to-bottom in the stack, and for a thin surface meant to conform to an underlying body (icing on a donut, cloth on a character, a decal/sticker/coating), a Shrinkwrap (or other conforming/projecting) modifier must sit ABOVE a Solidify (thickness) modifier in the stack -- if Solidify runs first, the extruded 3D volume gets Shrinkwrapped as a whole and collapses/distorts onto the target instead of the thin 2D surface snapping cleanly to it before being thickened.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 58:40-59:50, a Shrinkwrap modifier placed BELOW Solidify in the stack causes the icing mesh to flatten and distort onto the donut; dragging Shrinkwrap above Solidify immediately fixes it, letting the flat surface conform first before thickness is added.
rejected_alternative: Placing a conforming/projecting modifier below a thickness modifier in the stack for any surface meant to snap onto an underlying body first
reason: Modifier order is not cosmetic -- a thickness modifier applied before conforming operates on the wrong (already-3D) geometry, producing a collapsed or distorted result instead of a thin shell that follows the target surface.

claim: For a uniform sculpted deformation across an irregular perimeter or region (raising/lowering a rim, seam, or bead evenly) rather than an uneven hand-brushed result, paint a Sculpt Mode mask (M) with Front Faces Only enabled over the target region, invert it (Ctrl+I) if needed so the intended area is unmasked, then apply a Mesh Filter (e.g. Inflate) by dragging in the viewport -- the filter applies its mathematical deformation uniformly across the entire unmasked region in one gesture, rather than through repeated manual brush strokes that tend to leave lumps and divots.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 68:40-74:15, a mask painted along the icing's bottom rim (Front Faces Only, then inverted) isolates that region, and the Inflate Mesh Filter dragged across the viewport swells the entire unmasked rim outward with even, constant thickness in a single operation.
rejected_alternative: Manually sculpting a uniform raised/lowered feature with repeated individual brush strokes
reason: Manual brush strokes vary in pressure and coverage, producing uneven lumps and divots across a feature that needs to read as uniform (a rim, a seam, a piped edge); mask-isolate-then-filter applies one mathematical operation evenly across the whole isolated region instead.

claim: Geometry Nodes' Distribute Points on Faces (Poisson Disk mode, with a Distance Min threshold to prevent overlapping instances) feeding into Instance on Points, with the instanced mesh plugged into the Instance socket and combined with the base mesh via Join Geometry, scatters copies of a reference mesh across a target surface's topology without physically duplicating polygon data for each instance -- the scatter stays driven by editable distribution/density/scale/rotation parameters rather than being baked into static geometry.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 101:00-105:15, a Distribute Points on Faces node (Poisson Disk, Distance Min set) feeds Instance on Points, with a separate sprinkle mesh as the Instance input, combined with the icing mesh via Join Geometry to scatter sprinkles across the donut's icing surface.
rejected_alternative: Manually duplicating and placing individual copies of a small repeated element (sprinkles, rivets, scattered debris, foliage) by hand across a surface
reason: Manual duplication bakes the placement permanently and doesn't scale to hundreds/thousands of instances, while a points-distribute-then-instance graph keeps density, scale, and rotation as live editable parameters and avoids storing full polygon data per instance.

claim: Building a turned/cylindrical hard-surface part from a 2D profile (extrude upward, scale outward, fill the base face) and then bevelling selected parallel edge loops with Clamp Overlap enabled (C during the bevel) locks the bevel radius at the point where adjacent bevels would otherwise intersect, preventing self-intersecting/overlapping face artifacts as the radius grows toward neighboring geometry -- finishing with Merge by Distance (M) cleans up any coincident vertices left from the profile-fill step.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 176:50-181:20, a 2D circle profile is extruded and scaled into a cylindrical form, parallel edge loops are selected and bevelled with Clamp Overlap (C) enabled to prevent self-intersection as the bevel radius approaches neighboring edges, finished with Merge by Distance.
rejected_alternative: Bevelling edge loops without Clamp Overlap enabled on a part where the bevel radius may grow large enough to approach neighboring geometry
reason: Without Clamp Overlap, a bevel radius that grows toward an adjacent bevel or edge produces overlapping/self-intersecting faces instead of stopping cleanly at the collision point, breaking manifold topology on parts meant to shade and subdivide cleanly.
